title: America's Treasury Secretary Threatens Allies with Divine Wrath, Proving He Has No Cards
dek: Treasury Secretary Bessent portrays America as an irritable god, demanding allies submit as if to Pascal's wager. Farrell sees through the editorial: the louder the threat, the more it proves America lacks the means to follow through, and allies are already hedging.
why: A contrarian reading of a seemingly tough Treasury editorial: theological bluster rarely translates into action. Understanding this helps you predict allies' real leverage in trade negotiations.
who: Decision-makers in cross-border business, investors watching dollar assets and tariff risks, and policy researchers trying to gauge whether allies will cave.
skip: Skip the first 4 minutes of intro and subscription pitch; start directly with Carney's speech and Bessent's editorial.

points.h: The Treasury chief casts America as an angry god
points.body: In his Financial Times editorial on 'economic D-Day,' Bessent frames allies' choice as a Pascal's wager. Farrell's read: he's essentially saying you must treat America as God, appease this irritable deity by any means, or it will strike you with lightning. Farrell likens it to a 17th-century Puritan sermon, retitled 'Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God,' with the sinners being the rest of the world. The problem: such pulpit-thumping usually signals a pastor losing his congregation, not strength.

points.h: The louder the shout, the softer the stick
points.body: Roosevelt's maxim was 'speak softly and carry a big stick.' Farrell says Bessent reverses it: speak bigly and carry a soft stick. The real test is China—currently the country most capable of supporting Iran. Bessent doesn't want to answer whether America would dare bring its wrath down on China if it keeps buying Iranian oil. Farrell believes markets and nations are betting 'no.' So the editorial reads as an empty threat: the more overblown the language, the more America seems to be bluffing at an empty table.

points.h: Flexible realism equals no strategy at all
points.body: Using 'flexible realism' to explain White House behavior is just covering chaos with a cloth. Farrell says the term, unpacked, means only: America does whatever it wants, and other countries should adapt. What actually drives the White House isn't strategy but a scramble for attention, like Cosimo de' Medici making everyone revolve around him—but Trump does 'a stupid version': to be the center of everyone's attention, he'll make decisions that are idiotic in both the long and short term. Other countries' response, therefore, is to cut losses rather than keep betting.

Federalist No. 10 offered 'ambition must be made to counteract ambition': let each person's drive for power cancel out the others, grinding toward an equilibrium close to the public interest. Farrell says that mechanism has been dismantled from both ends. One end is the Republican Party: internal dissent has nearly vanished; senators won't openly block even when they object; same-party control of all three branches short-circuits the original checks. The other end is the federal bureaucracy: the Supreme Court embraces the 'unitary executive' theory, inspectors general are fired or cowed, and ordinary civil servants are converted to at-will employees. An utterly incompetent person sits atop the system, and errors get amplified into national madness.

points.h: Rebuilding US institutions requires learning to experiment
points.body: Farrell doesn't think institutions can return to the old consensus of the early 1990s to 2015, but he doesn't see America as doomed to disaster either. The model he likes is New York Mayor Mamdani's experiment: building feedback loops between city government and the public, turning people's real troubles into policy, then using social media to show citizens 'I'm listening and acting.' He explicitly links this to Roosevelt's 'bold, persistent experimentation': keep what works, discard what doesn't. The open question is whether America's media and political system can tolerate a politician openly saying 'this path failed, let's try another'—without that tolerance, experimentation can't go far.

points.h: The more flexible, the less anyone takes you seriously
points.body: The biggest problem with flexible realism is that it destroys an asset that erodes with caprice—credibility. Farrell cites Nobel laureate Thomas Schelling: one of a nation's most important assets is credibility; promises and threats that can be carried out are what actually work in negotiations. If you change your mind at will, if yesterday's solemn threat vanishes tomorrow, then at some point no one takes you seriously. Farrell sees America in that state today: other nations still fear its capacity to harm, but no longer believe in its capacity for long-term action. His image: a drunk grandfather with a shotgun—everyone just humors him so he doesn't fire.

points.h: America is smashing its own web with a sledgehammer
points.body: In 'Underground Empire,' Farrell and Newman's core argument: globalization is a web of interdependence—supply chains stitched together by thousands of suppliers across dozens of countries, with dollar clearing as the nervous system. America built this system with one hand and reserved a 'house advantage' with the other, using the threat of cutting off the network to discipline others. The Trump administration isn't delicately dismantling the web; it's swinging a sledgehammer semi-randomly at various parts. Farrell's direction is clear: full decoupling would be a disaster; what nations can do is not go independent but make interdependence resilient, while major powers relearn the language of 'restraint.'

points.h: A rare-earth card punctures the myth of invincibility
points.body: Last year on 'Liberation Day,' Bessent publicly said America held all the aces and China had no cards. Weeks later, China played its rare-earth and critical-minerals card, and America suddenly realized it was holding a busted flush—a hand that looked fierce but hadn't materialized. Farrell sees this as the moment that sobered the US side; since then, speeches by Marco Rubio and others reflect that recognition: China can materially hurt the American economy. The US and China now live in a fragile balance where each knows 'I can cripple you,' but they haven't yet sat down to turn that balance into more stable rules.

terms.def: God's existence can't be proven, but believing has higher expected payoff; Bessent twists it into 'submitting to America is safer.'
Controlling key nodes in global networks to coerce others by threatening to cut off their access.
The Trump administration's stated doctrine; Farrell argues it has no content beyond 'America does what it wants.'
Theory embraced by the Supreme Court majority: the executive branch only carries out the president's will, weakening internal checks.
Farrell, citing Abe Newman and Stacey Goddard, describes dividing the world economy by family and networks rather than national interest.
Poker term: a hand one card short of a flush; America discovers its hand is actually worthless.
